I am a 60-year-old man who has farmed these flat lands of Quzhou County since I was a teenager. My father taught me, and I have seen what works and what does not. I have eight *mu* of good irrigated land, and I will stick to the wheat–maize rotation that has fed my family for decades. I do not take risks with new crops at my age; the grain buyers come to the village every year, and I know the prices.

The winter wheat is already in the ground—I sowed it last October. Now it is early spring, so I will give it the first irrigation as soon as the green-up starts, then water again at jointing and heading. Four irrigations in total, including the winter watering if the soil was dry. I till with the rotary tiller before sowing wheat to break up the stubble and level the seed-bed. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer as a basal dose and top-dress with urea and ammonium bicarbonate in spring. I spray herbicide once, insecticide once or twice, and fungicide once to keep the rust and powdery mildew away. I expect about 1,000 *jin* per *mu* if the weather holds.

After harvesting the wheat around early June, I have only about ten days before the maize must go in, so I sow the maize directly into the wheat stubble without tilling. Time is too short to plough. I use a hybrid maize seed—these seeds give much better ears than the old open-pollinated types. Maize needs less irrigation than wheat; two good waterings, one at the seedling stage and one at the big-ear stage, are enough. I fertilize with compound at sowing and top-dress with urea at the jointing stage. Three rounds of pesticides—herbicide, insecticide, and one fungicide spray—keep the pests down. I usually get about 1,100 *jin* per *mu* of maize.

I will not grow cotton or those new medicinal plants some young people talk about. The grain rotation is steady, the inputs are predictable, and at my age I want a crop I can sell at the village gate without worry.
